newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Nov 21.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Nov 21.

text.p: THE DOMINION
A Maori trust has conditionally bought the old Museum of New Zealand building in Buckle Street, Wellington, in a deal understood to be worth about $7 million. Page 1.

Air fares look set to increase by up to three percent in time for the Christmas rush. The increases are blamed on rising aviation fuel prices. Ansett New Zealand chief executive Kevin Doddrell said on Wednesday his airline was lifting fares by three percent, effective from December 15, because of increasing costs. Air New Zealand and Qantas also confirmed on Wednesday they intended to raise fares for international and domestic routes. About 100 airline members of the International Air Transport Association met in Switzerland earlier this week and decided to increase fares to counter a rise in aviation fuel. An Air NZ spokesman said the transport association wanted all members to pass on

Informal coalition talks this week should have "broken the back" of the negotiations by Monday, NZ First leader Winston Peters said on Wednesday. Peters and other NZ First negotiators met National and Labour representatives, including Labour leader Helen Clark, in a series of informal discussions on Wednesday. "We covered over 10 issues today and I think from all reports that progress was very good," Peters said. Formal negotiations, which deal with areas of disagreement highlighted by the informal meetings, are due to resume next week. Page 2.
Labour transport spokesman Harry Duynhoven has issued car crash data that he said the Land Transport Safety Authority and Transport Minister Maurice Williamson should have made public. Page 2.

In less than four years, Ceramco Corporation has slumped from a blue-chip darling of the investment set to a beleaguered loss maker, without a leader and two directors short of a board. Ceramco reported a $1.63 million loss for the six months to September 30 and chairman David Appleby was unable on Wednesday to give a positive short-term solution to the problem. He said that provided there was no further deterioration in the apparel trade, it would take 12 to 18 months to get the Bendon-Hickory lingerie division contributing significantly to earnings of the group. The share price closed on Wednesday at $1.16 compared with a $9.50 high in 1993. Page 13.

A Californian sawmiller has announced plans to move his multi-million-dollar business to Wanganui. Sawmill owner John Cran said on Wednesday he was moving a $12 million mill from Corning, California to a new industrial estate in Wanganui. Two "boutique" sawmills and a bark-processing business are interested in following Crane to Wanganui. Page 13.

Coles Myer's annual meeting in Sydney was confirmation of a shift in board power toward a "trans-Tasman troika" made up of Brierley Investments, the Australian Myer family and former executive chairman Solomon Lew, the Australian Financial Review newspaper said on Wednesday. Brierley Investments owns 6.8 percent of Coles Myer, Australia's largest retailer, and Brierley chief executive Paul Collins was elected to the board on Tuesday at an acrimonious, six and a half hour meeting. Page 13.
Ongoing restructuring costs and pressure on interest margins made ANZ Group's New Zealand profit after tax fall 6.2 percent to $153.7 million in the year to September. Page 13.
Air New Zealand has received 98 percent acceptance for its 3-for-11 share offer. At $2 a share, it is aimed at raising $242 million to reduce debt. Page 13.
THE NEW ZEALAND HERALD

Coalition talks took a new twist on Wednesday when NZ First leader Winston Peters held a private meeting with Labour leader Helen Clark. The pair met alone for an hour at Parliament, in a session which some advisers at first denied had taken place. Peters said later on Wednesday he expects his caucus to reach a consensus decision on which of the Labour or National agreements it prefers, probably in less than a week.

The Serious Fraud Office says there are no grounds to justify an investigation into allegations of serious fraud made by Tui Milk Products shareholders opposed to the company's merger with Kiwi Co-operative Dairies.

United States President Bill Clinton on Wednesday gave new assurances that American subsidies would not target major New Zealand dairy markets in Asia. Instead, he said, the Dairy Export Incentive Programme would attack only price-cutting by heavily subsidised European dairy produce.

Education spending has become an obstacle in coalition talks between NZ First and Labour. If the two are unable to compromise, the funding issue could prevent a final agreement being reached. Labour finance spokesman Michael Cullen this week indicated that unless Labour could come close to delivering on its health and education promises, it would give up on the talks.

Ceramco Corporation, unveiling a slump to a $1.63 million loss in the September half-year, forecast on Wednesday that it would do no better than break even in the full year. A return to profit was forecast for the 1998 financial year.

ANZ Bank New Zealand has paid its Australian parent a $430 million dividend, the first in seven years, after reporting a steady profit for the September year. The bank reported a pre-tax profit of $231.5 million, down slightly from last year's $234 million.

Power New Zealand's main council shareholders have decided not to sell their key seven percent stake in the Takapuna-based electricity distributor. They have rejected an offer from Mercury Energy and, instead, have struck a deal with Utilicorp which gives the United States company pre-emptive rights over the shares, should the councils later choose to sell, in exchange for a guaranteed minimum price.

News that NZ First leader Winston Peters had called a 5 p.m. press conference rapidly reversed the fortunes of the soaring New Zealand dollar on Wednesday afternoon. The kiwi had climbed to an eight-and-a-half year-high of US71.63 cents, before retreating to finish at US71.2 cents.
